claim: WO-0010 acceptance criterion 11 is not met. The criterion asserts a universal invariant -- 'for every dt value WaveScheduler.Tick accepts without throwing (every finite dt >= 0, however large) ... the while loop is guaranteed to terminate in a finite number of iterations, because each iteration strictly increases _timeUntilNextSpawn by the fixed positive _interval. ... No dt value can reach the loop and fail to terminate it.' Both the invariant and its stated justification are false against the delivered implementation. The justification fails because `_timeUntilNextSpawn += _interval` is an IEEE-754 binary32 addition into a float field, and binary32 addition does not strictly increase its left operand: when _interval is smaller than half an ulp of _timeUntilNextSpawn, the sum rounds back to _timeUntilNextSpawn exactly and the iteration makes no progress at all. The invariant therefore fails for a large but perfectly finite, non-negative dt, which DtGuard accepts by design. Concretely, with the default test scheduler used throughout WaveSchedulerTests.cs -- Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f) -- the call `scheduler.Tick(1e8f, buffer)` enters the loop and never leaves it, calling into.Add(...) on every iteration. That is precisely the non-terminating loop with unbounded allocation into the caller's buffer that WO-0010's goal statement exists to eliminate, reached through a value the new guard passes rather than one it rejects. Separately, criterion 11 also requires the implementer to STATE the invariant; a full-text search of Assets/Core and Assets/Tests for 'invariant' and 'terminat' returns no statement of it in any XML doc, comment or test. Criterion 11 is thus neither stated nor satisfied, and the verification step reported it satisfied with no defect. I am not asserting a fix: the correct remedy may be a code change (compute the due-spawn count arithmetically, or bound the loop) or an amendment of criterion 11 by its author to the dt range over which it actually holds. That choice is the author's and engineering's, not mine. What I am asserting is that criterion 11 as written cannot be signed off against the code as delivered.
evidence: Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs:67-75 -- `_timeUntilNextSpawn -= dt;` then `while (_timeUntilNextSpawn <= 0f) { into.Add(...); spawned++; _timeUntilNextSpawn += _interval; }`. _timeUntilNextSpawn is a float field (line 20), so every += rounds to binary32 on the store; RyuJIT does not retain extended precision across a field store, so the rounding is guaranteed, not incidental.

Worked case, binary32, fully deterministic. Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f), dt = 1e8f. 1e8 = 390625 x 2^8 is exactly representable. 1f - 1e8f has exact value -99999999; the binade of that magnitude is [2^26, 2^27) so ulp = 2^(26-23) = 8; the neighbours are -100000000 (distance 1) and -99999992 (distance 7); the result rounds to -100000000. Loop condition -1e8 <= 0f holds, into.Add runs, then -100000000 + 2 has exact value -99999998, whose neighbours are the same pair at distances 2 and 6, so it rounds back to -100000000. The field is bit-identical after the increment. The loop cannot terminate and appends without bound.

General threshold: the increment is fully absorbed once _interval < ulp(_timeUntilNextSpawn)/2, i.e. once |_timeUntilNextSpawn| >= 2^25 x _interval, and can stall earlier by round-half-to-even from |_timeUntilNextSpawn| >= 2^24 x _interval. For _interval = 2f that is any dt at or above roughly 6.7e7 seconds; for _interval = 0.5f, roughly 1.7e7. In every such case dt is finite and non-negative and passes DtGuard.RequireFiniteNonNegative unchallenged.

Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs:20 -- `if (!float.IsFinite(dt) || dt < 0f)`. The guard rejects exactly NaN and the two infinities. Criterion 11 claims those are 'exactly the values capable of preventing termination'. They are not; they are the values that prevent termination by producing a non-finite accumulator. Absorption is a second, independent route to the same non-termination, through finite values only, and the criterion does not account for it.

Criterion 11 additionally requires the invariant be STATED. Grep of Assets/Core and Assets/Tests for 'invariant' returns only Assets/Core/Combat/WeaponStats.cs:19 (an unrelated DPS invariant); grep for 'terminat' returns only Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WaveSchedulerTests.cs lines 35, 58, 237, 241, all of which concern the non-finite case and the bounded test buffer, none of which states the general finite-dt termination invariant. No statement of criterion 11's invariant exists in the delivered code or tests.

No existing or new test passes WaveScheduler.Tick a large finite dt. The largest finite dt exercised anywhere in Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WaveSchedulerTests.cs is 201f (SpawnPositionsStayInsideTheConfiguredWidth, line 163). The region where the invariant fails is untested, which is why it was reported satisfied.

Ready-made regression test for the ratchet, using machinery already present in the file and requiring no new test infrastructure: with `var buffer = new BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer();` (WaveSchedulerTests.cs:38) assert that `Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, buffer)` completes and returns a finite count. Against the code as delivered this fails fast and deterministically with BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException at 1000 appends rather than hanging -- the same fail-fast technique criterion 10 already mandates. It fails before the fix and passes after, whatever the fix turns out to be.

Reachability, stated honestly rather than inflated: this is not reachable from Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs:45, because Time.deltaTime is never 1e8. It is reachable from any caller that chooses its own dt, which includes Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim, and it is reachable in full from the criterion's own words, which say 'however large'. I am challenging the criterion's satisfaction, not claiming a shipped-build hang.
